Let me analyze the teaching examples more carefully to identify the correction rules.

Looking at Example 1 (2025-01-29):
- History: prices rising from 75.94 to 81.67 over 18 days
- Model forecast vs true outcome divergence pattern:
  - Days 1-10: Model is slightly below reality (underestimating the continued rise)
  - Days 11-15: Model becomes significantly above reality (divergence of 4-6)
  - Days 16-20: Major divergence (7-9 points above)
  - Days 21-25: Even worse (10-11 points above)
  - Days 26-30: Most severe (12-15 points above)

Looking at Example 2 (2025-01-28):
- Similar pattern but starting from 75.19
- Model forecasts also appear too high in the latter half

Looking at Example 3 (2025-01-27):
- Starting from 73.00
- Same pattern of model being too high in days 11-30

Looking at Example 4 (2025-01-24):
- Starting from 71.98
- Days 11-30 also show model being too high

Looking at Example 5 (2025-01-23):
- Starting from 71.56
- Days 11-30 show the same issue

Let me look at the sentiment as well:
Sentiment history in Example 1: [0.67, 0.33, 1.00, 0.33, 0.67, 1.00, 0.67, 1.00, 1.00, -0.33, 0.67, 1.00, 1.00, 1.00, 0.33, 0.67, 0.33, 0.33]

Looking at the pattern of errors:
The model seems to have a specific issue:


I've identified a systematic bias in the forecast model. When prices are rising, the model underestimates the momentum, and when prices are stable or declining, it overestimates future values. The divergence becomes more pronounced 11-15 days into the forecast, with differences growing from 4-6 points to potentially 12-15 points. Sentiment indicators like negative values (-0.33) and low positivity (0.33-0.67) correlate with increased model overestimation
